en: The Ritual Manual for the Practice and Visualization of the Lotus Samādhi, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Guōqīng Monastery during the Táng Dynasty.
Now, although the methods of ritual repentance are universally practiced, the procedures and visualizations are often incomplete or inconsistent. Or...
Having read the text of the repentance only superficially, one does not master even half of it;
or, one uses forceful effort to resist contemplation through principle,
resulting in a total lack of the spirit of diligent application.
Lacking the sequence for entering the gate,
they claim that the diligent practice of asceticism is not the cause of *nirvāṇa*; yet,
as for the ritual protocols for worship and recitation, their textual details are not lacking.
Because distracted emotions and heavy delusions make the practice of visualization difficult to accomplish, I have,
based on the Tiantai tradition, provided further detailed supplementation.
I have extracted the essential points so that one may form mental images in accordance with the words and cultivate thoughts in accordance with those images.
Contemplate each one as if it were right before your eyes,
so that not a single moment may be wasted and the practice of the Dharma may be accomplished.
Following the original text, these ten dharmas are enumerated in their entirety.
A summary of the essential principles:

First, regarding the purification of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), if there is no separate room, it may be performed within the same space provided that one is entirely free from personal belongings and can seek out [the requisites] externally.
Second, regarding the purification of the body, new clothing is required; however, old clothing is also acceptable if it has been newly dyed.
If one lacks these two superior methods for cleansing old [defilements],
then when making offerings through the three types of action or performing general prostrations to the Triple Gem,
it is not necessary to visualize each [deity] individually according to their respective directions.
One should simply contemplate one's own body and the Buddhas of the ten directions;
because the essence of the principle of true reality (dharmatā) is fundamentally without subject and object,
there is no thought of a worshiper or an object of worship.
This absence of subject and object is called the ocean of the Dharma-realm.
May all sentient beings together perceive this principle;
this is termed "entering together."
Next, one performs the visualization of transporting the incense, chanting until the ritual service is completed and the incense is used.
Next, one generates the thought that this mind does not arise,
yet it is able to transport [the offerings] to the ten directions.
Therefore, it is said: "In a single thought-moment.
The visualization states:
"May these incense and flowers pervade the ten directions."
They are regarded as a subtle and wondrous pavilion of light,
with celestial music, celestial precious incense,
celestial delicacies, and celestial precious garments.
The inconceivable dust of the sublime Dharma:
from each and every particle of dust emerge all particles of dust;
from each and every particle of dust emerge all dharmas.
Rotating without obstruction, they mutually adorn one another and reach before all the Three Jewels—
before the Three Jewels throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm.
In each and every one, my own body performs offerings,
pervading the entire dharma realm;
each and every instance is without confusion or obstruction.
Performing Buddha-works throughout the limits of the future, universally permeating the Dharma-realm,
may all sentient beings who receive this permeation give rise to the Bodhicitta,
together enter the state of non-arising, and realize Buddha-wisdom.
I beseech the Buddha: the nature of my three karmas is like empty space;
Śākyamuni is also thus.
He does not arise from the limit of reality for the sake of sentient beings.
Together with the assembly, they come to receive offerings.
Next, when inviting the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, simply change the names of the Munis and the descriptions of their places of origin.
Prior to the five verses of praise for the Buddha, perform the individual visualizations for each one separately.
Position yourself before the Triple Gem.
Next, recite the verse aloud while following the sound with your visualization:
"My own body and mind are fundamentally without birth or extinction."
Therefore, although it is praised as being like a shadow or an echo,
when performing the sixfold prostration to the Buddha at the moment the "single mind" (*ekacitta*) is chanted,
one must first pay homage with focused and utmost reverence.
For the sake of the practice, one should focus the mind on a single object.
Next, one should contemplate the subject and object as being the principle, focusing the mind on that single principle.
One should reflect thus:
The nature of the worshiper and the object of worship is empty and quiescent;
the mutual resonance of their paths is inconceivable.
My place of enlightenment is like a celestial jewel.
While the shadow-form of Śākyamuni appears,
my own shadow-form appears before the Tathāgata;
with head touching his feet, I take refuge and pay homage.
Within the manifested image of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna,
my own body is manifested before him;
the rest is as described in the previous visualization.
The visualization for the various Buddhas of the body and the emanated bodies is the same as above.
Within the manifestation of the Buddhas of the eastern direction,
I likewise manifest before all those Buddhas.
This applies to every single direction throughout the ten quarters.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are all to be contemplated in the same manner.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas, including their śarīra relics and images, is like empty space.
The deeds of transformation as he dwells in the world are inconceivable;
before manifesting each of these transformative acts,
I take refuge in and pay homage to them all.
The wondrous Dharma is the true emptiness of the Dharma-realm, like space;
the eternally abiding Jewel of Dharma is inconceivable.
I appear as reflections before all these Jewels of Dharma.
There are none who do not take refuge in them and pay homage.
Within the reflected images of each and every one of those bodhisattvas—
even down to those in the lower directions— Śāriputra and the other śrāvakas previously visualized as being originally all Buddhas.
Because this is explained from the beginning, it is called "Śrāvaka.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, in order to extinguish obstacles, prostrates by touching his feet; the rest is as above.
[I pray] for myself and all sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have been constantly obstructed by the heavy sins of the three karmas and six sense faculties.
They do not see the Buddhas,
they do not know the essential way out,
and merely following the cycle of birth and death, they do not understand the sublime principle.
Although I now understand this, I am still hindered by all manner of grave offenses shared with all sentient beings.
Now, before the Buddhas of the ten directions, including Samantabhadra,
I take refuge and repent on behalf of all sentient beings.
I pray that you grant your protection so that all obstacles may be extinguished.

Regarding the seventh practice, the Repentance of the Ten Minds of Adversity and Favorability, it is said: "From beginningless time, I and all sentient beings have, due to the influence of craving and false views..."
Internally, they harbor notions of a self and persons; externally, they associate with evil friends and do not rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another’s merit.
They commit a multitude of transgressions through the full extent of their three karmic actions.
Although the actual deeds may not be numerous, their evil intent pervades them all.
Day and night they continue without interruption;
they conceal their faults and do not wish for others to know them;
they fear neither the evil realms nor possess a sense of shame or dread of wrongdoing.
Having previously denied cause and effect,
I now, before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Great Master Samantabhadra,
take deep faith in cause and effect and give rise to profound shame and remorse.
Giving rise to great fear,
they openly confess and repent, severing the continuity of their [unwholesome] mind;
they resolve upon the bodhicitta, abandoning evil and cultivating goodness.
Diligently restrain the three karmas to reverse former grave transgressions;
rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of virtue in ordinary beings and sages alike;
and be mindful that the Buddhas of the ten directions possess great merit and wisdom.
You are able to rescue me and all sentient beings from the ocean of the two deaths and place us upon the shore of the three virtues.
Since beginningless time, we have not known that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent.
Having extensively committed various evils,
they now realize emptiness and stillness in order to seek bodhi for the sake of sentient beings.
Extensively cultivate all virtues and universally sever all evils.
May Samantabhadra, out of compassion, graciously accept us.
Next, regarding the repentance of the six sense faculties, one must briefly understand the text as it appears.
The textual characteristics encompass the ten types of mental states regarding the adverse and the favorable; even if there are omissions,
within the four repentances, seeing [the mind] as impure regarding bodhi and so forth constitutes the horizontal conceptualization of self and person.
Vairocana contemplates the emptiness of the nature of transgressions;
all the World-Honored Ones are the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Within the latter four types of repentance, there is the arousal of a mind of sympathetic joy.
By these causes and conditions, they bring about ultimate purity.
This severing of the continuity of the mind and turning toward Samantabhadra and all the World-Honored Ones constitutes the arousal of the bodhicitta for the sake of sentient beings.
Each text for repentance fully encompasses the three karmas.
These include the cultivation of merit to compensate for faults, the confession of transgressions,
and the disclosure of errors.
"Facing falling into the evil realms and giving rise to great fear," and so forth;
this refers to fearing the evil realms, feeling shame and remorse,
and having faith in cause and effect.
In all recitations of the words of repentance, one must add a contemplation of the facts to break through the mind of attachment.
Upon reaching the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses, one should contemplate both fact and principle in their totality to repent before the mind of views.
If one wishes to further abbreviate, one may omit the three faculties of eye, ear, and nose.
It may also be used at times;
however, because the three faculties of tongue, body, and mind are [the result of] karma, they cannot be [omitted].
Even if the first three faculties were entirely omitted, [it would still be improper].
Furthermore, one will not lose [the practice], and the general meaning of the ten minds of the forward and reverse order will be attained.
One should exhort all Buddhas of the ten directions; by the power of their Dharma-eye, they will know me and see me.
One should exhort all Buddhas,
praying only that they may remain for a long time and turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma;
wherever they are born, one should always be able to offer such exhortation.
I rejoice in every single hair’s breadth of merit, whether mundane or sagely, throughout the ten directions;
may this merit bring joy to all who behold it.
Therefore, I rejoice.
I dedicate all my merit— be it as small as a single hair— from time immemorial until this very day and throughout the limits of the future,
including that derived from repentance, entreaty, and sympathetic joy.
All are identical with the Dharma-realm; together with all sentient beings, one shall accomplish the Buddha-way.
The essential substance of the vow must preserve the eradication of sins and removal of obstacles, opening and manifesting the Dharma-gates to fulfill the Four Great Vows.
All others must accord with bodhi.
When one wishes to practice the Way, one must further establish the correct visualization:
this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is just like the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
The Triple Gem of the ten directions fills the void.

Next, one visualizes the bodies of the Triple Gem of the ten directions revolving around the Dharma seat; their mental nature is quiescent and extinguished, appearing as reflections throughout the ten directions, with the sound of the sutra resonating like an echo.
Visualize that the mind is like a dream and the Brahma-voice is likewise.
For each of the three refuges, visualize the Three Jewels at each of the three locations simultaneously with the prostrations.
Although the initial text simply mentions the "ten directions," [the visualization should be expanded accordingly].
The mind also encompasses these three aspects.
From the point of repentance downward, whenever it is said that one pays homage to the Three Jewels,
one must in each instance separately give rise to the three perceptions.
First, prostrate three times with the head touching the ground:
first, to the Triple Gem of the ten directions;
second, to all the Triple Gems within the Lotus Sūtra.
Third, the Great Master Samantabhadra.
Regarding these three points, one seeks confession and so forth.
Furthermore, whenever flowers are scattered—specifically at the moment they are scattered before the words are spoken—[one should practice].
Having formed the visualization of the Three Jewels and the supreme visualization of Samantabhadra,
one next recites the words of confession and so forth.
As it says in the subsequent text:
Regarding "scattering flowers" and so forth, the mind refers to the flowers previously scattered.
If one is burning incense, it should be offered to the dharma-seat burner;
likewise, one should also visualize offering a burner for each of one's own bodies.
May [the fragrance] reach everywhere before each copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* throughout the ten directions, and even universally permeate all Three Jewels.
When burning incense in the hand-incense burner, first add the incense;
then, having taken hold of the burner, give rise to the appropriate visualization according to the specific purpose.
Thereafter, one should orally recite the phrases.
The text for seated meditation is brief;
it should be as described in works such as the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the *Ten Dharmas that Accomplish the Vehicle*.
For the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* repentance ritual performed at dusk and during the fifth watch of the night,
this abbreviated text is used when time is short: "I,
[Name], and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from beginningless time until now..."
Enshrouded by ignorance and deluded by perversion,
they extensively commit the ten evils, the four grave offenses, and the five heinous crimes through the six sense organs and three karmas;
this extends even to the ten major and forty-eight minor precept violations.
It is immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of verbal description.
The Buddhas of the ten directions eternally abide in the world, their Dharma sounds never ceasing;
wondrous fragrances fill all space, and the flavor of the Dharma overflows the void.
Pure radiance is emitted, illuminating and touching all things;
the eternally abiding wondrous principle pervades the entirety of space.
Since beginningless time, my six sense organs have been internally blind and my three karmas have been shrouded in darkness.
Not seeing, not hearing, not perceiving, and not knowing—
by these causes and conditions, they flow long through birth and death,
passing through the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
There will never be a time of emergence.
As the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is named Vairocana, pervading all places."
Therefore, you should know that there are no phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma;
yet I did not understand this and followed the flow of ignorance.
Thus, one perceives impurity within awakening and gives rise to fetters within liberation;
only now do I awaken to this, and only now do I repent.
Giving rise to great shame and remorse, and giving rise to great fear,
they recite and uphold the Mahāyāna, perform the threefold service of offering,
and take refuge in Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the World-Honored Ones.
Incense is burned and flowers are scattered as one discloses and repents;
all that has been committed through the six sense organs and three karmas is forever severed,
and the continuity of such acts shall not be created again.
By these causes and conditions, all that has been done by myself and all sentient beings of the dharma-realm throughout the three karmas and six sense faculties since beginningless time—
whether performed in the present, to be performed in the future, or performed by oneself, taught to others, seen, heard, or rejoiced in— [I now confess].
Whether remembered or not remembered, whether recognized or not recognized,
whether doubted or not doubted, whether concealed or revealed—
having performed the repentance that is ultimately pure, one takes refuge in and pays homage to the Triple Gem.
The Ritual Manual for the Practice and Visualization of the Lotus Samādhi: A Supplemental Rite.
